extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, and teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and explanatory criteria about how students reason with and learn mathematical proof, including cognitive constraints (mental models, working memory), pedagogical strategies (scaffolding, representation, practice), and the use of pragmatic reasoning schemas in selection tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental models three-stage reasoning process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning proceeds in three stages: (1) construction stage — build models representing information in the premises; (2) description stage — devise a concise description (conclusion) that asserts something not explicitly stated; (3) validation stage — search for alternative mental models (counterexamples). If no alternative model is found the conclusion is considered valid; if one is found, return to the description stage and repeat until all possible models of the premises have been examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cycle construct→describe→validate when analysing or teaching deductive reasoning. Treat conclusions as tentative until alternative models have been sought; a conclusion is only secure when it cannot be falsified by any alternative model. Example: derive algebraic forms from premises and test for alternative constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic competence to comprehend logical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful model construction depends on the learner's linguistic competence to correctly understand logical vocabulary (e.g., and, or, not, if, none, some, all) in the premises and thereby construct appropriate models of those premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and build students' understanding of quantifiers and connectives before or while engaging them in proving tasks (e.g., seven-year-olds often fail syllogisms because they do not understand quantifiers correctly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working memory capacity as a limiting factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of mental models that must be constructed and the figural arrangement of terms determine difficulty because working memory must hold and manipulate representations; limitations lead to failure to consider counterexamples and validation errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and supports that account for working memory limits (evidence: performance drops on three-model problems; adults with short response time perform like children). Consider cognitive load when sequencing tasks and when expecting students to keep multiple models in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaffolded proving tasks to reduce unnecessary memory load
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students with a small, specified set of relevant premises (scaffolded tasks) so they do not expend working memory on identifying irrelevant premises and can focus on logical structure and idea development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scaffolded tasks early in instruction to help students build logical skills; progressively remove scaffolds as students gain competence so they learn to select relevant premises themselves. Example: giving the two defining premises for multiples of 3 and 6 before asking for a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent information in equivalent, easier-to-manage forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformulate premises into concise, equivalent representations (e.g., algebraic expressions) to reduce working memory demands and facilitate combination of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach strategies for algebraic reformulation and symbolic condensation of premises; this reduces memory footprint and supports construction of more complex mental models (example: rewriting definitions of multiples as 3l and 6k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make efficient use of visual records and diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Create or use diagrams and other visual records to integrate separate sources of information and off-load working memory by providing an external record to consult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to produce and refer to visual records when givens are separated from diagrams (e.g., geometry tasks with separate diagram and givens). Train students to integrate textual givens with diagrams rather than holding them mentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and internalization of proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated practice helps students become more efficient in operating short-term processing and storing representations; internalizing logical structures of proof methods (e.g., proof by contradiction) reduces working memory demand during application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include deliberate practice aimed at internalizing common proof structures so students can apply methods with less cognitive overhead. Note empirical findings of spontaneous improvement with retesting and practice effects without feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ritualized emphasis on form over substance (anti-pattern: two-column obsession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing instruction exclusively on ritualized formats (e.g., the two-column proof form) can make proof-writing a memorized ritual and obscure the substantive logical chain that guarantees truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize understanding of logical relations and coherent chains of reasoning over rote practice of surface formats. Use forms when helpful, but not as an end in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pragmatic reasoning schemas (permission and obligation) to facilitate selection tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoking pragmatic reasoning schemas (clusters of rules tied to everyday goals such as permission and obligation) can markedly improve performance on selection-type deductive tasks by mapping if-then statements to familiar schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing selection tasks or related instruction, include semantic cues that evoke permission/obligation schemas (e.g., modals like can/must/may) to aid performance. Empirical evidence: permission-framed tasks yield much higher correct rates than abstract versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission schema production rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Core permission schema summarized as four production rules: Rule 1: If action A is to be taken, then precondition B must be satisfied. Rule 2: If action A is not to be taken, then precondition B need not be satisfied. Rule 3: If precondition B is satisfied, then action A may be taken. Rule 4: If precondition B is not satisfied, then action A must not be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach or make explicit these rules when invoking permission mappings; mapping an if-then conditional onto a permission schema changes which inferences are salient and can facilitate correct reasoning in selection tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation schema training improves transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief training in an obligation schema (detailing the nature of obligations and procedures for checking violations, with examples and four-rule procedures mapped onto p, not-p, q, not-q) improves subjects' performance on problems interpretable in terms of obligation and even on some abstract problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement short, concrete training modules that explicate obligation schemas (examples, procedural checks). Empirical protocol: two-page booklet with example obligation statements and procedures increased correct performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional sequencing: exploit schemas then remove cues for transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin instruction with selection tasks that provoke students' existing pragmatic schemas to build confidence and skill, then progress to tasks without such cues (more abstract forms) to promote transfer and increased difficulty handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences using empirically supported progression: contextualized/schema-evoking tasks → less-facilitated/abstract tasks. Anticipate that tasks without schema cues will be more difficult and require scaffolding or explicit strategy instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differences between selection tasks and mathematical proof tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Although selection tasks share logical structure with proof methods (e.g., contraposition, counterexample), important differences exist (e.g., selection tasks present particular cases to check, while proofs often require constructing counterexamples or selecting relevant premises from community knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume direct transfer from success on selection tasks to capability on proving tasks; research and instructional design should examine and bridge cognitive requirements (e.g., constructing vs checking cases) to support transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify premises when applying mental models to proving tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental models theory accounts for solution of proving tasks when a set of premises has been specified (either given in the task or selected by the reasoner); if premises are unspecified, the reasoner must select relevant accepted statements to construct a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing mental-model-based strategies, start with tasks that explicitly provide premises; teach students how to revise and expand the set of premises as needed and reapply the mental-model cycle after each revision.
